title: Diameter of Binary Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: recomputing depth from scratch per node versus a single combined post-order pass.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary tree, return the length (measured in number of edges) of the diameter of the tree, the longest path between any two nodes, which may or may not pass through the root.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root of a binary tree"],["Output","The diameter, the longest edge-count path between any two nodes"],["Key Insight","The longest path passing THROUGH a given node equals that node's left subtree depth plus its right subtree depth"],["Constraints","Up to 10^4 nodes"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Longest path between any two nodes, not necessarily through the root\"","Every node is a potential \"peak\" of the longest path passing through it; computing depth via post-order recursion lets a running maximum be tracked as a side effect"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

The diameter is the longest path between ANY two nodes, and every such path has some single node as its highest point (where the path turns from going down-left to down-right, or is entirely one-sided). At that peak node, the path length equals its left subtree's depth plus its right subtree's depth. Checking this at every node, while computing depths anyway, finds the overall answer.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Longest Hallway Through Any Junction in a Building
blocks.text: Picture a building where every junction connects a left wing and a right wing. The longest possible hallway through any single junction equals that junction's left wing's depth plus its right wing's depth; checking every junction while touring the building anyway finds the longest hallway overall.

blocks.caption: The longest path through a node equals its left depth plus its right depth

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] (1 with children 2,3; 2 with children 4,5)
Diameter = 3. The longest path goes 4-2-1-3 or 5-2-1-3, both with 3 edges (through node 2, depth 2 on the left of node 1 counting 4/5, plus depth 1 on the right).
Example: tree = [1, 2]
Diameter = 1, the single edge from 1 to 2.
5. How Should We Think?

Before separately computing depths from scratch at every node to check each one's potential path length (redundant, repeated work), notice that computing depth via a SINGLE post-order pass already visits every node's children's depths first, letting a running maximum diameter be updated as a side effect at zero extra traversal cost.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The longest path passing through a specific node as its peak equals that node's left subtree depth plus its right subtree depth (each measured in edges, so subtree depth in nodes minus one, or equivalently just summing the two child depths in nodes directly gives the edge count of the combined path).

Observation 2: The tree's overall diameter is the MAXIMUM of this "left depth plus right depth" value across ALL nodes, since the true longest path's peak is one specific node.

Observation 3: A single post-order depth computation ALREADY visits every node's children's depths before computing its own, making it free to also check and update a running maximum diameter at each node during this same pass.
This leads to a single post-order recursive depth function that also updates a shared running maximum using left depth plus right depth at every node.
6. Brute Force Solution
For each node, separately compute its left and right subtree depths from scratch (a fresh recursive call each time), tracking the best combined value found.
Why the code is written this way

items: Calling a fresh depth computation at every node directly implements the "left depth plus right depth at every node" idea.
This recomputes the same subtree depths over and over across different ancestor nodes, costing O(n squared) in the worst case (a skewed tree).

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) worst case (a skewed tree), since each depth call re-traverses its subtree.
Space: O(h) recursion depth.
Limitation: combining the depth computation and the diameter update into a SINGLE post-order pass avoids ever recomputing the same subtree's depth twice.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Maintain a single shared "best diameter found so far" variable. Define one recursive function depth(node) that: returns 0 for a null node; otherwise, recursively computes the LEFT depth and RIGHT depth (each already updating the shared best diameter during their own recursive calls), updates best using left depth plus right depth for the CURRENT node, and returns 1 plus the larger of the two depths (as usual). This single function computes both depth AND diameter simultaneously in one pass.
Use one post-order recursive function that computes depth and updates a shared running maximum diameter simultaneously.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for [1,2,3,4,5] (1 with children 2,3; 2 with children 4,5)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Node","Left depth","Right depth","Updates best with"],"rows":[["4 (leaf)","0","0","0"],["5 (leaf)","0","0","0"],["2","1 (via 4)","1 (via 5)","2, new best"],["3 (leaf)","0","0","0"],["1 (root)","2 (via 2)","1 (via 3)","3, new best, FINAL answer"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since a post-order traversal computes each node's children's depths before the node itself, folding "update the running diameter using left depth plus right depth" directly into this SAME traversal means every node's subtree depth is computed exactly once, and every node is still checked as a potential peak of the longest path, correctly finding the true maximum diameter with no redundant recomputation.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each node's depth computed exactly once.
Space: O(h) recursion depth.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Recompute depth from scratch per node","O(n squared) worst case","O(h) recursion depth","Correct, but redundant recomputation."],["Single pass, depth plus diameter together","O(n)","O(h) recursion depth","The expected, efficient solution."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Diameter of Binary Tree is the classic example of folding an auxiliary computation (tracking a running maximum) into an existing recursive traversal (depth), avoiding a separate, redundant pass.
Common Mistakes

items: Calling a separate, fresh depth() function at every node, causing the O(n squared) redundant recomputation the brute force suffers from.
Confusing the diameter (edge count) with a node count, an off-by-one source of bugs if depths are not combined correctly.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single node tree","Diameter is 0 (no edges at all)."],["A tree where the longest path does not pass through the root","Still correctly found, since every node is checked as a potential peak, not just the root."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "fold the diameter update into the existing depth recursion, do not compute depth separately per node" demonstrates the key optimization insight clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "longest path between any two nodes, not necessarily through the root", think: combine depth computation and a running maximum update into one post-order pass.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you also report WHICH two nodes achieve the diameter, not just its length?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree and Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum, both build on this same post-order depth-combination technique.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The redundant recomputation approach costs O(n squared) worst case; folding the update into a single post-order pass costs O(n), the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: fold an auxiliary running-maximum update into an existing post-order recursive traversal.
Core Idea: the longest path through any node equals its left depth plus its right depth; the diameter is the maximum of this value across all nodes.
Time: O(n squared) worst case for the brute force, O(n) for the combined single-pass approach.
Most Important Observation: depth computation and diameter tracking can be combined into one traversal, avoiding redundant work.
Interview Difficulty: a classic medium-level recursive tree problem.
One line memory trick: left depth plus right depth, tracked as you go.
